z-m-27-01.title: How many ways are there to hand out 6 candies?
z-m-27-01.topic: The number of ways to hand out candies: whether candies are told apart and whether empty hands are allowed
z-m-27-01.goal: Realize that the sentence 'the number of ways to hand out' alone does not fix a single answer, and rewrite the problem by stating for yourself the conditions needed to decide the answer (whether candies are told apart, whether empty hands are allowed).
z-m-27-01.material: We want to hand out all 6 candies to three people, 갑, 을, and 병. 갑, 을, and 병 have fixed names, so they are different people. Ways of handing out candies are counted by the result 'who received what.' If the result is the same, it is the same way, and the order of giving candies is not counted. The problem is just one sentence. "How many ways are there to hand out 6 candies to three people?"
z-m-27-01.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough before finding the answer
z-m-27-01.thinking.1: Predicting how the number of cases changes when the conditions change
z-m-27-01.thinking.2: Checking by building cases whose conditions are fixed
z-m-27-01.thinking.3: Rewriting an ambiguous problem so that it has a single answer
z-m-27-01.prereq.0: Writing the cases as ordered pairs and listing them without missing any
z-m-27-01.prereq.1: The product rule and the sum rule (level of the early part of the 'counting cases' unit in high school Common Mathematics)
z-m-27-01.prereq.2: The H2 in the school-level assignment is only a difficulty label in this production plan, not a school grade assignment. Assume the basic ideas of the counting-cases unit have already been learned.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.prompt: For this one sentence alone to have a single answer, what more must we absolutely know? Choose all that apply.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.hint.0: Separate, as if drawing a line, the conditions already written in the problem text from the conditions that are not written.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.hint.1: Fix one count for (갑, 을, 병) so that the result stays the same, and think about which condition, if changed, would make that result different or impossible.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.o.a: The ages of the three people 갑, 을, and 병
z-m-27-01.s.s1.r.a: Age has nothing to do with how many ways there are to divide. Think about which information changes the way of counting.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.o.b: Whether the 6 candies are told apart from each other
z-m-27-01.s.s1.r.b: You noticed that depending on whether the candies are told apart, even the same distribution of numbers can be counted as different ways.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.o.c: Whether candies are given one at a time in turn or all at once
z-m-27-01.s.s1.r.c: This problem has been set up to count only the result and not the order of giving. It is already a fixed condition.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.o.d: Whether it is fine if one of the three people gets no candy at all
z-m-27-01.s.s1.r.d: You noticed that whether the cases where someone receives 0 are included changes the very list of possible cases.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.o.e: Whether 갑, 을, and 병 are different people
z-m-27-01.s.s1.r.e: It is already written that they have fixed names. Separate the information that is given from the information that is missing.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.explain: There are two pieces of missing information. Depending on whether the candies are told apart, even when the numbers are the same, like (갑 4, 을 1, 병 1), it becomes a different way if the candies received are different. Also, the possible cases change depending on whether an empty hand is allowed. That the people are told apart and that the order of giving is not counted have already been given.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.prompt: Let's fix the case where all 6 candies are the same kind and all three people receive at least 1 each. Enter 6 different ways. (the number 갑 receives is a, the number 을 receives is b, the number 병 receives is c)
z-m-27-01.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the number one person receives, and look at what the sum of the numbers the other two people receive must be.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.hint.1: Are (4,1,1) and (1,4,1) the same way? Check against the problem text's standard that 'if the result is the same, it is the same way.'
z-m-27-01.s.s2.ok.c1: All three people have 1 or more.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.fail.c1: All three people must receive at least 1 each.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.ok.c2: Candies cannot be split, so the numbers are integers.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of candies must be an integer.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum of the numbers the three people receive must be 6.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.explain: Under this condition there are 10 ways in all. (1,1,4), (1,4,1), and (4,1,1) are counted as different ways because the person who gets 4 candies is different. This is because the three people are told apart. Even the same group of numbers (1,2,3) splits into 6 ways depending on who receives how many.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.prompt: This time suppose the 6 candies are all of different flavors, and it is fine for a person to get none. Compared with dividing candies of the same kind with empty hands allowed (28 ways), what happens to the number of ways?
z-m-27-01.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one distribution from the same-kind case, (4,1,1), and work out directly into how many ways that distribution splits when the candies are told apart.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.hint.1: Think of deciding, candy by candy, 'which of the three people gets it,' and count how many times that choice is repeated.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.o.a: It decreases. Because the candies must be told apart, the condition is stricter.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.r.a: Telling candies apart does not make any possible distribution disappear. Look at into how many ways the same distribution of numbers splits.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.o.b: It is the same, 28 ways. Because the number of candies and the number of people stay the same.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.r.b: Even if the numbers of candies and people are the same, in the same (4,1,1) distribution it is a different way if who gets which candies is different.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.o.c: It increases. Because one distribution splits into several ways.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.r.c: You pointed out that once candies are told apart, one distribution breaks into several ways.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.o.d: We cannot know without working out what happens.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.r.d: You can compare the sizes without calculating everything, by looking at just one distribution and how many ways it splits into.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.explain: If the candies are all different, each candy chooses one of three people, so it is 3 to the 6th power, that is, 729 ways. That is far more than the 28 ways for the same kind. This is because each of the 28 splits into several ways. For example, even (4,1,1) alone splits into many depending on which 4 candies 갑 receives.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.prompt: Revise the first sentence and write the problem in two different interpretations so that each has one answer. You do not have to find the answers (how many ways), but write them so that it is clear which conditions you added.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.hint.0: Fix the two pieces of missing information you chose at first, one at a time, and put them into the sentence.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.hint.1: The two interpretations must differ in at least one condition. Decide which condition to change and write it.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Can you say in one line what condition differs between the two interpretations you wrote?
z-m-27-01.s.s4.selfAssess.1: When you read each interpretation, can you tell whether the candies are the same or told apart?
z-m-27-01.s.s4.selfAssess.2: In each interpretation, can you tell whether it is fine for someone to receive no candy?
z-m-27-01.s.s4.model.0: Interpretation 1) All 6 candies are the same kind, and it is fine for a person to receive 0. Interpretation 2) All 6 candies are different flavors, and it is fine for a person to receive none.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.model.1: It can be written as the number of ways to divide 6 identical candies so that all three people get at least 1 each, or as the number of ways to divide 6 candies that are told apart so that no one is left out.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.modelNote.1: This answer chose the third combination of conditions (told apart + everyone gets 1 or more). Even if the combination differs, it is valid as long as the conditions are clear.
